read.sections.0.heading.source: Your feed is chosen for you
read.sections.0.heading.back: Your timeline is chosen for you

read.sections.0.text.source: People post far more than anyone could see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes in your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you watched, liked or skipped before, and guesses what you will want to see. Apps aim for different things. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people if they were happy with what they saw. A feed can be useful. In the made-up town of Maplebrook, Lena's feed found her a free video lesson on writing stories. Ravi watched many football videos, so his feed showed him mostly posts about the new sports field.
read.sections.0.text.back: People post far more than anyone could see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes into your timeline. An algorithm is a series of steps a computer follows. An algorithm learns from what you watched, liked or passed over before, then guesses what you want to see. Each app has a different aim. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people whether they were satisfied with what they saw. A timeline can be useful. In the made-up town of Maplebrook, Lena's timeline found a free video lesson about writing stories for her. Ravi watched many football videos, so his timeline mostly showed posts about the new sports field.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: People post more than you could ever see. So many apps use an algorithm. An algorithm is a set of steps for a computer. It picks posts from what you watched before. read.sections.0.simpler.back: People post more than you could see. So many apps use an algorithm. An algorithm is a series of steps for a computer. An algorithm chooses posts from what you watched before. Each app has a different aim. Some count how long you watch. Some ask whether you liked it. A timeline can help. In the made-up town of Maplebrook, Lena's timeline found a free lesson about stories for her. Ravi's timeline showed posts about the new sports field.

read.sections.1.heading.source: A rumour can spread faster than the truth
read.sections.1.heading.back: A rumour can spread faster than the truth

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study of Twitter. They looked at about 126,000 news stories shared from 2006 to 2017, each checked by fact-checking groups. On Twitter in those years, false stories spread further and faster than true ones. They were often more surprising, and people shared them, not only robot accounts. The study looked at what people chose to share on one site, not at how feeds pick posts. This matters before an election, when people need correct facts to vote. In Maplebrook, a rumour said the vote had moved to Friday. It was shared 900 times in one day, and the correct notice only 60 times.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study about Twitter. They looked at about 126,000 news stories shared from 2006 to 2017, each of which had been checked by fact-checking groups. On Twitter in those years, false news spread further and faster than true news. False news was often more surprising, and humans shared it, not only robot accounts. The study looked at what people chose to share on one site, not at how timelines choose posts. This matters before an election, when people need correct facts to cast their votes. In Maplebrook, a rumour said the vote had been moved to Friday. The rumour was shared 900 times in one day, while the true notice only 60 times.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 2018, MIT researchers in the US studied news stories on Twitter. The stories were from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread faster than true ones. They often seemed surprising. People shared them, not only robots. The study looked at what people shared on one site. It did not study how feeds pick posts. This matters in an election. In Maplebrook, a rumour said the vote moved to Friday. It got 900 shares. The true notice got 60.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 2018, MIT researchers in the United States studied news on Twitter. Those stories were from 2006 to 2017. False news spread faster than true news. False news often felt surprising. Humans shared that news, not only robots. The study looked at what people shared on one site. The study did not research how timelines choose posts. This matters in an election. In Maplebrook, a rumour said the vote had been moved to Friday. The rumour was shared 900 times. The true notice was shared 60 times.

read.sections.2.text.source: Some people worry that feeds put each of us in a filter bubble, where we only see one side. Ravi saw mostly posts for the sports field, and Lena saw mostly posts for the library. But a review of many studies found that real filter bubbles are less common than many people think. Since 2024, a European Union law has said that very large apps must explain how their feeds choose posts. They must also offer a feed that isn't based on what they know about you. You can help too: follow different sources, and check before you share.
read.sections.2.text.back: Some people worry that timelines put each of us in a filter bubble, where we only see one side. Ravi mostly saw posts supporting the sports field, and Lena mostly saw posts supporting the library. But a review of many studies found that real filter bubbles are rarer than many people think. Since 2024, a European Union law has said that very large apps must explain how their timelines choose posts. Those apps must also provide a timeline that is not based on what they know about you. You can help too: follow different sources, and check first before sharing.

watch.summary.source: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. On many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you don't see. So when you scroll, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone built a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? It tries to show you posts that will keep you interested, so you keep scrolling. Experts in the video say this isn't always a good thing. Your feed is carefully chosen. It is not a full view of the world. Knowing how your feed is chosen can help you think about what you see.
watch.summary.back: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a series of instructions that tells a computer program what it must do. On many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. The algorithm also decides which posts you don't see. So when you scroll the screen, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone made a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? The system tries to show posts that keep you interested, so you keep scrolling. The experts in this video say this is not always good. Your timeline is carefully chosen. That timeline is not a complete picture of the world. Knowing how your timeline is chosen can help you think about what you see.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Elections and politics can be painful or dangerous topics for some learners. Keep the discussion on made-up Maplebrook. educatorNotes.0.source: The research in section 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018): about 126,000 cascades of news stories on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted over 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true stories took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the gap held with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and stories that fact-checkers had investigated (contested stories, not all posts). It measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need separate study.
educatorNotes.0.back: The research in section 2 is by Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018): about 126,000 chains of news spreading on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted more than 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, and each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true news took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the difference remained even with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and news that fact-checkers had investigated (disputed stories, not all posts). The study measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need to be studied separately.

educatorNotes.1.source: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; don't reduce them to one motive. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review found echo chambers much less widespread than commonly assumed and no support for the filter bubble idea. The European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force 16 November 2022, applying in full from 17 February 2024, and earlier to very large platforms (over 45 million monthly users in the EU), four months after the Commission designated them; they must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one not based on profiling, and assess risks such as the manipulation of elections.
educatorNotes.1.back: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; don't simplify them to one motive. For example, YouTube's help page names watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”, not only watching time). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review found echo chambers far rarer than usually assumed, and found no support for the filter bubble idea. That European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force from 16 November 2022, applying in full since 17 February 2024, and earlier for very large platforms (more than 45 million users a month in the European Union), four months after the European Commission designated them; those platforms must explain the main settings of their recommendation systems, provide one system not based on user profiles, and assess risks such as election manipulation.

educatorNotes.2.source: Paper version of the activity: write the six posts on cards and sort them into two piles, “Likely to spread fast” and “Less likely”. There is no score; ask for reasons. Ask why the correct notice spreads more slowly, and who could help it spread.
educatorNotes.2.back: Paper version of this activity: write the six posts on cards and group them into two piles, “Good chance of spreading fast” and “Smaller chance”. There is no score; ask for reasons. Ask why the true notice spreads more slowly, and who could help spread it.
